background: Dual sourcing is a classic supply-chain model where a firm can replenish from a slow cheap supplier and a fast expensive supplier. The model is simple to state but hard because orders placed today arrive after different deterministic lead times, so the state includes a multi-period pipeline from each supplier. When the lead-time difference is one, the dynamic program has much more tractable structure. When the gap is two or more periods, the exact optimal policy has resisted a clean characterization for decades. This makes the problem a good fit for ORdős Problems: the modelling choices are already settled, the objective is a standard infinite-horizon inventory cost, and there are strong heuristic and asymptotic policies. Xin and Goldberg gave theoretical support for Tailored Base-Surge policies by proving asymptotic optimality when the regular-source lead time grows while the express-source lead time is fixed. That result resolves an important large-lead-time question, but it does not characterize the exact finite-lead-time optimal policy. The remaining open problem is structural: describe the optimal policy, or prove sharp non-asymptotic guarantees for a simple policy class, when the two lead times differ by at least two.
open_problem: Characterize the exact optimal policy for the periodic-review dual-sourcing inventory model with deterministic regular and express lead times whose gap is at least two, or prove sharp finite-lead-time optimality-gap guarantees for Tailored Base-Surge or related simple policies.
known_results: For lead-time gap one, the state and dynamic program simplify enough to yield tractable structural results. For larger gaps, dual-index policies and Tailored Base-Surge policies have strong numerical performance. Xin and Goldberg prove that a simple Tailored Base-Surge policy is asymptotically optimal as the regular-source lead time tends to infinity with the express-source lead time fixed, giving a theoretical foundation for the heuristic in the regime where the dynamic program is most intractable. The exact optimal policy for fixed finite lead-time gaps at least two remains unknown. Later survey and inventory-asymptotics work clarifies why large-lead-time asymptotic optimality does not automatically provide a usable exact policy for moderate lead times.

where_posed.text: The long-standing finite-gap structural problem is discussed in the dual-sourcing inventory literature; Xin and Goldberg identify the model as having resisted exact solution for more than forty years while resolving the large-regular-lead-time TBS asymptotic question.
where_posed.location: Introduction and model discussion of Xin and Goldberg 2016.

progress.summary: Tailored Base-Surge is now known to be asymptotically optimal in a large-lead-time regime, but no exact finite-gap optimal-policy characterization is known for lead-time differences at least two.

counterexample_rationale: Small finite lead-time and finite-demand-support instances can refute conjectured threshold or index structures through dynamic programming. A full characterization must handle an unbounded inventory/pipeline state.
alphaevolve_rationale: Search can map optimal actions in truncated dynamic programs, infer switching surfaces, and locate counterexamples to proposed structures. It is less suited to proving asymptotic or infinite-state optimality without analytic support.

literature.synthesis: Dual-sourcing inventory has a clean economic interpretation and an unusually difficult state space. Earlier work proposed dual-index and Tailored Base-Surge policies and demonstrated strong computational performance. Xin and Goldberg supplied the major theoretical advance by proving TBS asymptotically optimal as the regular lead time grows. Their result supports the intuition that a constant slow-source base flow plus a fast-source order-up-to correction becomes nearly optimal when the slow pipeline is long. The open finite-gap problem remains because optimality for $L_r \to \infty$ does not tell us the exact Bellman structure for fixed $L_r-L_e \ge 2$, where pipeline imbalances and expediting decisions interact. A successful solution would likely identify monotonicity, convexity, or low-dimensional sufficient statistics for the dynamic program, or else show that no simple threshold/index form can be exact.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Begin with two- or three-period lead-time gaps and finite-support demand, compute truncated Bellman equations, and look for monotone comparative statics or switching-curve regularity. Analytic approaches may use L-convexity, pipeline-state aggregation, vanishing-discount limits, or lower bounds tied to lost-sales/queueing asymptotics.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed exact policy must be checked against Bellman optimality for the infinite-horizon discounted or average-cost problem with explicit state variables. A claimed non-asymptotic guarantee must state the parameter regime and compare to the true optimal policy, not only to another heuristic.
